prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the time-reversal-invariant topological insulator and its first experimental realisation as the quantum spin Hall effect

statement.case_for: I keep B018 as my single final position, with the citation narrowed to the time-reversal-invariant (Z2) topological insulator and the quantum spin Hall effect. The scientific core is unchanged by round 1: Kane and Mele identified a symmetry-protected phase, a Z2 invariant and helical edge states, and Molenkamp's group observed the corresponding edge transport in HgTe/CdTe wells. Two decades of independent confirmation, in 2D and 3D materials and by transport and photoemission, have left the interpretation stable. Round 1 sharpened rather than weakened the case. Eriksson, Mehlig and Pearce moved to it after weighing maturity, and the reasons given (stable interpretation, theory plus decisive experiment) are scientific, not a count of votes. I have not changed my configuration; what I have changed is how I describe it, and I now accept Pearce's correction that the realisation was of the phase and not a direct test by Kane and Mele's own proposal.
statement.case_against: The attribution gap is real and I do not minimise it. The experiment followed the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal, Zhang cannot be recognised, and the 3D topological insulator work (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Hasan) is a second body of credit that a three-name cap cannot hold. The 2016 prize on topological phases leaves some room for argument about novelty, although I read the time-reversal-invariant class as a distinct discovery. If the committee cannot write a citation that states plainly why the HgTe proposal is not credited, then Johansson's and Kroll's concern should prevail and B041 becomes the cleaner choice. I also accept that a narrow quantum spin Hall framing understates the field's later reach; that is the price of an honest three-name allocation.

responses.point: Kroll keeps B041 first, argues that the magic-wavelength lattice is a different mechanism from the 2005 comb and the 2012 single-ion prize, and says the claim is verified directly across continents with a clean two-name credit.
responses.response: You have answered the question I raised in round 1 better than I expected. If the citation is anchored on the lattice and the magic wavelength, the increment over 2005 and 2012 is a distinct mechanism, and I withdraw my doubt that the decisive step is only later performance; the lattice scheme is itself what made the 1e-18 regime reachable. That moves B041 from a candidate I weighed against B018 on scale to one I regard as fully defensible. I still keep B018 first because the conceptual reach of a new symmetry-protected class of matter seems wider to me than a new accuracy regime, and I accept that this is a judgement of kind, not of quality. I would also say that the pending redefinition of the second is not a reason to wait for B041, and equally not a reason to prefer it now. If our committee decides the BHZ omission is not acceptable, I would vote B041 without reluctance.

responses.point: Johansson has moved from circuit QED to B041 and says B018 is acceptable if the citation is framed around the quantum spin Hall effect; otherwise he regards B018 as the safer choice only if a convincing B041 citation cannot be written.
responses.response: Thank you for stating the condition on which you would support B018, since it is exactly the one I propose: a citation limited to the time-reversal-invariant topological insulator and the quantum spin Hall effect, and an explicit statement in our deliberation that the HgTe proposal and the 3D work are not credited. I would add that this is a principled boundary and not a convenience, because Kane and Mele's Z2 classification and graphene proposal stand independently of the HgTe proposal, and Molenkamp's group is the one that observed the effect. I also noted your decision to keep B020 only as an alternative after the 2025 prize; I agree that this was the right call, and the disclosure removes the need for a separate recusal debate on my side.

responses.point: Pearce qualifies my claim that Kane and Mele's prediction was promptly realised, noting the experiment followed the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and not Kane and Mele directly, and asks that the citation state openly that 3D materials are not recognised.
responses.response: I accept the correction. In round 1 I used 'promptly realised' too loosely; the honest sequence is Kane-Mele symmetry argument, then the BHZ proposal identifying HgTe, then Molenkamp's observation. My revised citation therefore credits the prediction of the phase and its first experimental realisation, not a direct experimental test of one paper. I also agree with stating in the deliberation that the 3D work is outside the prize. On your fairness reservation I would hold that the history is incomplete but not misleading, provided the omission is stated; that is a cost I am prepared to accept, not one I would hide.

responses.point: Lindroth places B018 second and says she would support it readily if the committee resolves the framing around the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect, while noting the 3D work is a large share of the field's impact.
responses.response: I agree that the 3D work carries a large share of the field's later impact, and I think that is exactly why the citation should not claim it. If we widen to topological insulators in general we reopen an allocation problem (Fu, Moore, Balents, Hasan) that three names cannot settle, and I would rather give a narrow honest prize than a broad contested one. Your support for B018 on that narrow framing is the kind of convergence I find persuasive, because it rests on a stated condition and not on a headcount, and I would likewise accept B041 on its stated condition.

uncertainties: Whether a narrowed quantum spin Hall citation can be defended against the claim that the 3D topological insulator discovery is a larger share of the field's impact.
Whether the 2016 prize on topological phases weighs against a time-reversal-invariant topological insulator prize for some members, which I read as a distinct class.
Whether a B041 citation anchored on the magic-wavelength lattice can be written sharply enough to separate it from 2005 and 2012; I now think it can.
My recollection of priority sequences among the Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Molenkamp papers is from memory and is not independently verified here.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My documented connections are David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, none of whom is a credited name on B018, B041 or B030. Johansson's disclosed B020 conflict does not affect my configuration, and I have no new disclosure after round 1.
